claims.text: The ductile-brittle-ductile transition in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is driven by non-monotonic APBE evolution coupled with changes in B2/FCC interface morphology.
At about 600°C, the FCC matrix develops near-stoichiometric Ni3Al-like L12 domains.
Near-stoichiometric L12 ordering at about 600°C maximizes the APBE.
B2/FCC phase boundaries become jagged or serrated near 600°C because of interfacial segregation and limited diffusion.
High APBE raises the energetic cost of forming antiphase boundaries and restricts dislocation cross-slip.
Restricted cross-slip forces planar dislocation slip in the brittle state.
Planar slip impinging on serrated B2/FCC boundaries produces stress localization and initiates microcracks.
At about 750°C, thermal disordering lowers L12 order and APBE and thereby restores cross-slip.
Aging at about 750°C smooths B2/FCC interfaces, reduces stress concentration, and restores ductility.
The critical transition occurs when the L12 order parameter falls below approximately 0.4-0.5 and B2/FCC interface-energy anisotropy is minimized.
The as-cast alloy has a ductile, random FCC matrix and smooth B2/FCC interfaces.
Aging for about 100 hours in the 550-750°C range induces L12 ordering and B2/FCC interface evolution.
The alloy is ductile after aging at 550°C, brittle after aging at 600°C, and ductile after aging at 750°C.
Yield strength peaks and elongation reaches a minimum at about 600°C.
TEM of the 600°C state will show a high density of highly ordered L12 precipitates and jagged B2/FCC interfaces.
At 750°C, L12 domains will have lower order and B2/FCC interfaces will be smoother than at 600°C.
Order hardening will produce higher hardness and modulus at 600°C than at 750°C.
The 600°C state will have a lower nanoindentation pop-in load than the 750°C state, indicating easier dislocation nucleation despite restricted subsequent motion.
The brittle regime begins when the L12 order parameter exceeds about 0.5 and interface roughness exceeds a critical value, typically between 580°C and 620°C.
Cross-slip behavior in FCC alloys is temperature dependent in a way relevant to the proposed mechanism.
